title: Satan, the Adversary
lead: The Hebrew word satan means "adversary." In most of the Hebrew Bible it names an ordinary opponent; in Job and Zechariah "the satan" is an accuser in God's court; in 1 Chronicles 21:1 Satan stirs David to count Israel; and in the New Testament Satan, the devil, is the great enemy of God and his people, defeated by Christ.

sections.b: In most of the Hebrew Bible satan is a common noun: the angel who blocks Balaam's road is "a satan" (Numbers 22:22), the Philistines fear David may become their satan in battle (1 Samuel 29:4), David calls his nephews his satan (2 Samuel 19:22), and God raises up satans against Solomon (1 Kings 11:14, 11:23). In Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3:1–2, "the satan" is a member of God's council who accuses, acting only with God's leave. 1 Chronicles 21:1 has Satan, without the article, stir David to count Israel where 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD did. In later Jewish writings the accuser becomes the leader of evil spirits, with names such as Belial and Mastema, and the New Testament speaks of Satan or the devil as the tempter (Matthew 4:1–11), the accuser thrown down (Revelation 12:9–10), and the enemy whose works the Son of God came to destroy (1 John 3:8).
